claims.claim: Le Guin says narrative prose going a long distance needs more muscle than fat, and recommends a thoughtful, careful choice of adjectives and adverbs.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)

claims.claim: Le Guin's Chastity exercise asks the writer to produce descriptive narrative prose without adjectives or adverbs, using only verbs, nouns, pronouns and articles.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)

claims.claim: Le Guin says the word suddenly seldom means anything at all and is a mere transition device.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: Suddenly seldom means anything at all

claims.claim: Le Guin says stating flatly that repetition is to be avoided goes right against the nature of narrative prose.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: repetition is the central means of achieving rhythm

claims.claim: In Le Guin's detached-author point of view, people and places may be exactly described but values and judgments can only be implied indirectly.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: values and judgments can only be implied indirectly
claims.page: chapter 7, 'Point of View and Voice', Detached Author

claims.claim: Le Guin says that in the detached-author point of view the author never enters a character's mind.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: The author never enters a character’s mind.
claims.page: chapter 7, 'Point of View and Voice', Detached Author

claims.claim: Le Guin calls the detached-author voice the least overtly and most covertly manipulative of the points of view.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: the least overtly, most covertly manipulative of the points of view
claims.page: chapter 7, 'Point of View and Voice', Detached Author

claims.claim: Le Guin says the world of a science fiction or fantasy story must be created and explained in the story, because the reader has no way of knowing it otherwise.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: must be created and explained in the story

claims.claim: Le Guin says crafty writers break information up, grind it fine, and make it into bricks to build the story with, rather than letting exposition form lumps.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: grind it fine, and make it into bricks

claims.claim: Le Guin says the story is not in the plot but in the telling, and that it is the telling that moves.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: The story is not in the plot but in the telling.

claims.claim: Le Guin opens Steering the Craft by saying the sound of the language is where it all begins and that the test of a sentence is whether it sounds right.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'The Sound of Your Writing', chapter one of Steering the Craft (2015), excerpted at Literary Hub
claims.quote: The sound of the language is where it all begins.

claims.claim: Le Guin says pace and movement depend above all on rhythm, and that the primary way to feel and control the rhythm of prose is by hearing it.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'The Sound of Your Writing', chapter one of Steering the Craft (2015), excerpted at Literary Hub
claims.quote: Pace and movement depend above all on rhythm

claims.claim: Introducing a passage of Zora Neale Hurston, Le Guin says the vocabulary is simple and familiar and that it is above all the rhythm that is powerful and effective.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'The Sound of Your Writing', chapter one of Steering the Craft (2015), excerpted at Literary Hub
claims.quote: the vocabulary is simple and familiar
claims.page: chapter one, note introducing example III

claims.claim: Le Guin says the sound of the names of places can be intensely expressive, citing Faulkner's Yoknapatawpha County and Tolkien's simple yet deeply evocative Middle-earth.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'The Sound of Your Writing', chapter one of Steering the Craft (2015), excerpted at Literary Hub
claims.quote: his simple yet deeply evocative Middle-earth
claims.page: chapter one, 'to think or talk about afterward'

claims.feature: other: prose that stops to be admired
claims.claim: Le Guin asks whether a novelist who visibly strives for striking or poetical prose, using unusual or archaic words, intensifies what is being said or distracts from it.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'The Sound of Your Writing', chapter one of Steering the Craft (2015), excerpted at Literary Hub

verdicts.note: Both limbs verbatim in ch.5: the 'thoughtful, careful choice of adjectives and adverbs' recommendation and the muscle/fat clause sit in one sentence of the raw djvu text.

verdicts.trueWording: descriptive narrative prose without adjectives or adverbs
verdicts.note: 'EXERCISE FIVE: Chastity' verbatim; the page names verbs, nouns, pronouns, and articles as the permitted parts of speech, exactly as claimed.

verdicts.trueWording: Suddenly seldom means anything at all
verdicts.note: Verbatim, and the following clause on the page is 'it's a mere transition device, a noise', supporting the second limb.

verdicts.trueWording: go right against the nature of narrative prose
verdicts.note: Claim sentence is verbatim on the page ('to state flatly that repetition is to be avoided, is to go right against the nature of narrative prose'); the supplied quote also appears verbatim later in the same chapter.

verdicts.trueWording: values and judgments can only be implied indirectly
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the Detached Author section, preceded on the same line by 'People and places may be exactly described' - both limbs present.

verdicts.trueWording: The author never enters a character's mind
verdicts.note: Verbatim sentence inside the Detached Author definition of ch.7.

verdicts.trueWording: the least overtly, most covertly manipulative of the points of view
verdicts.note: Verbatim; the page's subject is the detached-author voice, matching the claim's attribution.

verdicts.trueWording: The world of the story must be created and explained in the story
verdicts.note: Verbatim in ch.9; the 'no way of knowing' limb is supported two sentences earlier ('information ... that the reader has no way of knowing unless told').

verdicts.trueWording: break up the information, grind it fine, and make it into bricks
verdicts.note: Verbatim; the preceding sentence, 'Crafty writers (in any genre) don't allow Exposition to form Lumps', supports the lumps limb.

verdicts.trueWording: The story is not in the plot but in the telling
verdicts.note: Verbatim, immediately followed by 'It is the telling that moves.' Located under the subsection heading 'A DISCUSSION OF STORY' in ch.10, exactly as the page field states.

verdicts.trueWording: The sound of the language is where it all begins
verdicts.note: Verbatim opening of the Lit Hub excerpt, followed by 'The test of a sentence is, Does it sound right?'; the page states this is the first chapter of Steering the Craft.

verdicts.trueWording: Pace and movement depend above all on rhythm
verdicts.note: Verbatim, followed by 'the primary way you feel and control the rhythm of your prose is by hearing it - by listening to it.'

verdicts.trueWording: the vocabulary is simple and familiar
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the note that introduces example III (Hurston), followed by "it's above all the rhythm that is powerful and effective". The note reads 'In this one and the next', so it covers Hurston and the following Gloss passage too; the claim does not assert exclusivity, so no limb fails.

verdicts.trueWording: his simple yet deeply evocative Middle-earth
verdicts.note: Verbatim, in a passage that runs 'names ... can be intensely expressive' then 'Names of places, too: Faulkner's Yoknapatawpha County, Tolkien's haunting Lothlorien or his simple yet deeply evocative Middle-earth.' The 'intensely expressive' predicate is stated of names and extended to place names by 'too'.

Verbatim in the discussion questions; the same question ends 'Does it intensify what it's saying or distract you from it?', supporting the intensify/distract limb, and names 'a novelist or essayist who visibly strives to write striking or poetical prose'.
